analysis.title: Treasury Sells First 9-Day Bill Since July 2008 As Month-End Cash Gets Tight
key_insights: Treasury sold $15B of 9-day cash management bills (CMBs) on Nov 19, 2026 at a high rate of 3.910% and a 3.97x bid-to-cover, issuing Nov 24 and maturing Dec 3. It is the first 9-day bill since July 21, 2008 ($9B at 1.565%).
Only 11 auctions of this length appear in the TreasuryDirect record back to 1980.

On Oct 22 Treasury sold $25B of 10-day CMBs to bridge a few days when, per John Comiskey of Reverse Engineering Finance, the TGA was about to fall below the minimum set by Treasury's cash balance policy, even with nearly $1T in the account.

The Nov 19 bill covers month-end, settling the Tuesday before Thanksgiving and maturing just after the Dec 1 outflows. Treasury flagged it in the Nov 4 refunding statement as a 'potentially issuing a short-dated CMB' around the end of November.
Ultra-short CMBs have been rare: six of the past ten years had none.
Demand was solid. Indirect bidders took 45.8% of the bill (vs 18.3% in October) and dealers 52.0% (vs 77.6%).

Goldman's rates team expected reserve management purchases to restart this month at $10B. The New York Fed instead scheduled no reserve purchases between Nov 16 and Dec 11, extending a pause that began in mid-August.
The Fed is not adding reserves while Treasury refills the TGA toward a projected late-November peak of about $1.025T. The month-end gap is being filled with short-dated bills.
The government was $685.1B below the $41.1T debt limit as of Nov 13, a gap that is shrinking fast. Goldman and JPMorgan both expect the limit to bind around February.
After the limit binds, the TGA drains and must later be rebuilt quickly. Funding markets wobbled at that stage in 2019 and 2025. Goldman says reserves are 'at more of a cusp on the demand curve.'
The author expects a bumpier 2027 with more stopgap CMBs and a Fed that ends up resuming bill purchases.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Rate paid on $15B of 9-day bills, the first 9-day auction since 2008. It shows how short-term Treasury cash needs have become.
Demand was adequate for the $15B size.

macro_indicators.indicator: Treasury General Account (TGA) projected late-November peak
macro_indicators.interpretation: Treasury is rebuilding its cash balance while the Fed pauses reserve purchases, so reserves are not growing.
The gap is narrowing quickly. Goldman and JPMorgan expect the limit to bind around February.
The pause that began in mid-August continues, against Goldman's expectation of $10B of purchases restarting in November.
Goldman's expectation did not materialize, which leaves reserves tighter than it assumed.

tension_points.bull_case: Demand for the 9-day bill was solid, with a 3.97x bid-to-cover and indirect bidders at 45.8%. The author concedes it may be a one-off, since 'Maybe that's all today was.'
tension_points.bear_case: The Fed has paused reserve purchases since mid-August, and Treasury has needed two ultra-short CMBs in a month. The debt limit is expected to bind around February, after which the TGA rebuild has coincided with funding market stress (2019, 2025). The author calls this a preview of a bumpier 2027.
tension_points.what_invalidates: The New York Fed restarting reserve management purchases, which Goldman had expected at $10 billion this month, would ease the reserve squeeze. The scheduled pause runs through Dec 11.

theme_stances.key_argument: With the Fed not adding reserves and Treasury rebuilding the TGA, month-end cash gaps are being filled with very short bills, which points to tighter reserves than 'ample' implies.
theme_stances.evidence: the "ample" in ample reserves is doing a lot of work
